source_refs.note: Topic 8.3, printed pages 182-183: parenchyma and turgor pressure, collenchyma and sclerenchyma.

blocks.text: Supporting tissues maintain the structural integrity, support and flexibility of plants. They are parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma, xylem and phloem.

Parenchyma supports herbaceous plants and parts of larger plants. The parenchyma cells of the epidermis, cortex and pith absorb water, which creates an internal hydrostatic pressure, turgor pressure, that maintains the rigidity of the cells. Turgor pressure arises from the elevated osmotic pressure in the cell vacuole. The membrane around the vacuole, the tonoplast, has many active transport mechanisms that move ions into the vacuole even when the concentration inside is already higher than in the surrounding fluid. Because of the raised ionic concentration, water is drawn into the vacuole, giving turgidity and mechanical support to the plant's soft tissues.

Collenchyma cells are specialised cells grouped in strands or cylinders beneath the epidermis of young stems and leaf stalks and along the veins of leaves. They lack secondary walls; their primary walls are thickened at the corners by extra deposits of cellulose. They elongate as the stem or leaf grows lengthwise, and support the young parts of the plant in which secondary growth has not taken place.

Sclerenchyma also gives structural support. Its cells typically have thick secondary walls saturated with lignin, an organic compound that confers strength and rigidity, and most sclerenchyma cells are non-living. The tissue's main function is support. There are three types of sclerenchyma cell: fibres, sclereids and vessels. Fibres (tracheids) are elongated and cylindrical, found as compact bundles inside the xylem or as bundle caps. Sclereids are smaller than fibres and occur in seed coats and the shells of nuts, where they give protection. Vessels (tracheae) are long tubular structures joined end to end to form the long water-conducting pipes of the xylem.

blocks.alt: Three cell types. Parenchyma: rounded thin-walled cells each with a large blue vacuole. Collenchyma: angular cells with green thickened corners. Sclerenchyma: two long brown fibres with narrow lumens and two round brown sclereids with tiny lumens.

blocks.long_description: Parenchyma cells have thin walls and large vacuoles; ions pumped into the vacuole draw in water, and the turgor pressure keeps soft herbaceous tissue rigid. Collenchyma cells are living, with primary walls thickened at the corners by extra cellulose, and support young growing parts. Sclerenchyma cells have thick lignified secondary walls and are mostly dead; fibres, sclereids in seed coats and nut shells, and the vessels of the xylem belong here.
